edits.find:
Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis made by counting organ systems against the clock; hypotension is not required. Within minutes to hours of a likely allergen, skin or mucosal findings plus one more system (respiratory, gastrointestinal or cardiovascular) meet criteria. This boy has wheals and periorbital swelling (skin), throat tightness (respiratory) and cramps (gut) 30 minutes after amoxicillin, so this is anaphylaxis despite a normal blood pressure. The mechanism is IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, prostaglandins and leukotrienes. "No known drug allergies" does not argue against it: an earlier exposure sensitized him without a reaction, and re-exposure triggers the release.

The exception is angioedema without hives. Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or bowel wall with no wheals and no itch, from an ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema, is bradykinin-mediated, builds over hours and responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines. Rashes that arrive days into a drug or an infection are delayed reactions, not anaphylaxis.

edits.find:
Choose the precaution by how the organism travels. Droplets are 5 microns or larger and fall within 3 to 6 feet, so a surgical mask within that range is enough: N. meningitidis, H. influenzae type b, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza, adenovirus, pertussis. Airborne particles are under 5 microns and stay suspended, so they need an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room: tuberculosis, measles, varicella, SARS. Contact organisms spread by hands and surfaces and need a gown and gloves: MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, E. coli O157:H7, scabies, RSV. Gram-negative diplococci in CSF are meningococcus, so this infant needs droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.

Standard precautions apply to every patient and are never the added answer. Neutropenic precautions run the other way: they protect the patient from the environment rather than others from the patient.

edits.find:
One sentence in the physical examination is the whole question: he is calm when left alone and screams when picked up. That is paradoxical irritability — handling stretches inflamed meninges, so being comforted makes an infant worse. It is the meningeal sign of infancy, and it exists because nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski are unreliable under roughly 12 to 18 months.

Everything else in the stem is a negative that closes an alternative source. No cough or rhinorrhea closes the respiratory branch. A negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite in urine concentrated to a specific gravity of 1.030 closes the urinary branch — concentration is what makes the negative trustworthy. When the sources are eliminated one by one and a meningeal sign remains, the answer is the lumbar puncture.
